claims.text: The starting material consists of uncoated tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions embedded in a copper matrix.
A nanoscale, conformal nickel coating can be applied to tungsten surfaces by physical vapor deposition or an equivalent method before consolidation with copper.
Consolidation will be conducted below the boiling point of copper.
The intended fusion-reactor service environment involves temperatures of approximately 1000 K or higher and irradiation.
An interfacial nickel layer acts as a wetting enhancer at the tungsten–copper boundary.
Nickel reduces the interfacial energy between tungsten and molten copper.
Reduced W–Cu interfacial energy improves copper infiltration during consolidation.
Improved wetting strengthens bonding between tungsten and copper during consolidation.
Improved W–Cu wetting suppresses void nucleation and phase separation.
Suppressing voids and phase separation produces a more uniform W–Cu microstructure.
A more uniform W–Cu microstructure preserves thermal transport under irradiation.
A more uniform W–Cu microstructure preserves mechanical durability under irradiation.
Standard spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying of uncoated tungsten particles provides an existing fabrication baseline.
Relative to the uncoated fabrication baseline, nickel-coated tungsten will yield a lower void fraction.
Relative to the uncoated fabrication baseline, nickel-coated tungsten will yield more continuous W–Cu interfaces.
The nickel-coated composite will have improved thermal conductivity relative to the uncoated baseline.
The nickel-coated composite will have improved mechanical performance during service relative to the uncoated baseline.
Prolonged irradiation may cause nickel diffusion or intermetallic formation.
